presentingComplaint: Rapidly worsening pain, swelling and discolouration of the right lower leg over 24 hours with high fever and confusion.
history: Type 2 diabetic (HbA1c 9.4%) admitted 3 weeks ago at another hospital for an ESBL Klebsiella urinary tract infection treated with meropenem, discharged 10 days ago. Sustained a minor abrasion to the right shin 3 days ago. Over the last 24 hours the leg became exquisitely painful — far out of proportion to the modest skin changes — with fever, rigors and drowsiness. He is not on chronic steroids and is not neutropenic. This is presented as an MDR-risk host in whom empiric therapy must be broad and escalation planned, with early surgical source control the definitive intervention.
examination: Ill, toxic-looking, drowsy. Right lower leg tensely swollen with dusky erythema spreading proximally above marked skin lines, tense haemorrhagic bullae over the shin, and palpable crepitus. Skin anaesthetic centrally but surrounding tissue tender out of proportion. Serous 'dishwater' discharge from the abrasion. Pain wildly disproportionate to visible cellulitis; borders indistinct and advancing.
imaging: Bedside/CT of the limb: gas tracking along the fascial planes with fluid and fat stranding deep to the deep fascia; no drainable abscess. Imaging must not delay surgical exploration.
microbiology: Two sets of blood cultures drawn before antibiotics. Intra-operative tissue Gram stain: mixed flora with Gram-negative bacilli and Gram-positive cocci. Cultures at 48h grew ESBL-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae (meropenem-susceptible) plus MRSA — consistent with a type I polymicrobial NSTI in an MDR-colonised host, prompting escalation off piperacillin-tazobactam onto a carbapenem and retention of MRSA cover.
finalDiagnosis: Necrotizing fasciitis (polymicrobial, type I) with septic shock in an MDR-colonised diabetic host
citations: IDSA Skin and Soft Tissue Infections Guideline 2014
Surgical Infection Society Necrotizing Soft-Tissue Infections Guideline 2021
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e — Necrotizing Skin and Soft Tissue Infections
stewardship: Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency: source control by emergent, aggressive debridement is the single most important intervention and must not await imaging. Empiric antibiotics are broad-spectrum per IDSA — vancomycin (MRSA cover) PLUS piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem (Gram-negative/anaerobic cover) PLUS clindamycin for its antitoxin/anti-exotoxin and protein-synthesis-inhibiting effect. Given prior ESBL Klebsiella and recent hospitalisation, MDR risk is high, so carbapenem (meropenem) is justified up front here rather than piperacillin-tazobactam. Once tissue and blood cultures return (ESBL Klebsiella + MRSA), therapy is culture-directed: retain meropenem for the ESBL organism, retain vancomycin/linezolid for MRSA, and continue clindamycin until toxin-mediated shock resolves; de-escalate/narrow only when repeat debridements show no residual necrosis and the patient stabilises.
contraindications: Do not delay surgical debridement to obtain imaging or await culture results.
Avoid piperacillin-tazobactam as sole Gram-negative cover given documented ESBL history — use a carbapenem.
Dose-adjust vancomycin and meropenem for acute kidney injury; monitor levels.
edgeCases: LRINEC score has limited sensitivity — a low score does not exclude NSTI when clinical suspicion is high.
Pain out of proportion and rapid progression can precede any skin necrosis; early normal-looking skin is a classic pitfall.
Clindamycin adds antitoxin benefit but is not relied upon for definitive cover if local clindamycin resistance is high.
expectedMaiK: Rapidly progressive soft-tissue infection with pain out of proportion, crepitus/haemorrhagic bullae, systemic toxicity and fascial gas — necrotizing fasciitis requiring emergent surgical debridement plus broad empiric antibiotics, escalated for MDR risk.
